label: Illustrative layouts for planning practice. Not real buildings. Coverage from them is a MODEL ESTIMATE.

scenarios.description: One router in the corner of a 48 m2 flat. The bedroom is the far end.
scenarios.learn: Distance and two concrete partitions between router and bedroom. Move the router toward the middle.
scenarios.name: Small apartment

scenarios.description: Two floors with one router in a downstairs corner. The upper floor and the far side are weak.
scenarios.learn: A floor slab adds loss. Add an AP on the upper floor and compare coverage.
scenarios.name: Large home

scenarios.description: Three APs that all sit on channel 1 along a corridor, plus a neighbouring network on channel 6.
scenarios.learn: Co-channel interference: APs on the same channel share airtime. Run the channel plan.
scenarios.name: Office floor

scenarios.description: Brick classrooms on both sides of a corridor with three corridor APs at 5 GHz.
scenarios.learn: Brick walls cost far more than drywall. Corridor APs reach classrooms only through the doors.
scenarios.name: School building

scenarios.description: Metal racking forms long aisles. One AP in the office and one at the far end.
scenarios.learn: Metal blocks signal almost completely. Aisles between racks act like corridors.
scenarios.name: Warehouse

scenarios.description: Concrete guest rooms along a corridor with two corridor APs.
scenarios.learn: Concrete room walls leave the corridor APs reaching only nearby rooms. Consider one AP per few rooms.
scenarios.name: Hotel floor

scenarios.description: Open seating with the router behind the bar. A microwave and Bluetooth speaker share the 2.4 GHz band.
scenarios.learn: Interference sources raise the noise floor and lower SINR even when RSSI looks fine.
scenarios.name: Coffee shop

scenarios.description: Drywall wards along a corridor, a steel lined imaging suite and three corridor APs that all use channel 36.
scenarios.learn: Medical devices and clinical apps need dependable roaming. Walk a path down the corridor in Timeline and check the handoffs, then run the channel plan.
scenarios.name: Hospital ward

scenarios.description: A router downstairs, clients on both floors (TV, camera, console, laptop) and no AP upstairs.
scenarios.learn: Use Recommendations to see whether a mesh node upstairs beats moving the router.
scenarios.name: Smart home

scenarios.description: A flat between two others, with concrete party walls and three neighbour networks, two on the router's channel 6.
scenarios.learn: Shared concrete walls shield the signal but neighbours still raise the noise on channel 6. Run the SINR channel plan and compare.
scenarios.name: Apartment with neighbours

scenarios.description: A 30 m2 studio with one open room, a small bathroom and a kitchenette. The router sits by the sofa.
scenarios.learn: A small open space is easy to cover. The bathroom is the weak spot, so test the router position.
scenarios.name: Studio apartment

scenarios.description: A concrete shell condo with a living area on the left and two bedrooms and a bathroom on the right.
scenarios.learn: The concrete shell shields neighbours, but the drywall partitions still cost the bedrooms signal. Compare a central router with a mesh node.
scenarios.name: Two bedroom condo

scenarios.description: Three floors joined by a stairwell, with one router on the ground floor. Each floor up costs signal, except near the stairs.
scenarios.learn: A stairwell opening lowers the floor loss near it. Try a mesh node on the first floor landing.
scenarios.name: Three story house

scenarios.description: A ten person office: open plan on the left, a meeting room, a manager office and a server closet behind a metal door on the right.
scenarios.learn: A metal door makes the server closet a dead end for the AP. The meeting room is the test of a video call.
scenarios.name: Small office
